Senses.Note: One named-person sense covers Lü Dongbin, Lü Chunyang, and the True Person Pure Yang. Criticism of longevity and alchemy, positive sword portraiture, and changed conduct after meeting Huanglong are different recorded stances toward the same figure, not separate people or lexical senses. The encounter witnesses abbreviate the other figure to Huanglong. They do not name Huanglong Huinan or connect Lü to Huinan's later Three Barriers, so that former related-term link has been removed; the likely Huanglong Huiji identity remains a context question for the dedicated roster pass rather than a silently asserted link here.

Senses.Explanation: This expression means to seek fire and anchors the repeated answer, “the fire-boy comes seeking fire.” Qinglin Shiqian first gives the answer to Xuanze. “Will ultimately fall apart” is Nanquan Puyuan’s judgment on Magu Baochi’s display as movement driven by external force. In the case Magu circles the seat, strikes his staff, and stands. Zhangjing approves, while Nanquan rejects him: Zhangjing is right, but Magu is not; what is moved by wind ultimately decays. Fenyang Shanzhao preserves the exchange in verse. Yuanwu Keqin explains that motion attributed to wind remains within the compounded body and asks where clarification of the mind-source lies. Wansong Xingxiu treats Nanquan’s judgment as the pivot beyond simple right and wrong. Wuyi Yuanlai also contrasts conditioned effort ending in decay with immediate accord.
Senses.Note: The line does not condemn all activity. In the Magu case it diagnoses a display as wind-driven and therefore conditioned.
